summary: Willy Bang-Kaup was a linguist and scholar of Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at KU Leuven under Charles-Joseph de Harlez de Deulin, later teaching Germanistics there (1895–1914) before professorships in Frankfurt (1917) and Berlin (1918).

Willy Baruch worked in Indology, Buddhist studies, and sinology. He studied at Berlin, Leipzig, and Bonn (Ph.D. by 1937) under Heinrich Lüders, Friedrich Weller, and Willibald Kirfel, and taught Manchu at INALCO from 1933 to 1935.

Willy Foy, an Indologist and linguist, earned his Ph.D. at Leipzig (1892–1895) studying under Ernst Windisch and Karl Brugmann. He served as the first director of the Rautenstrauch-Joest Museum (1901–1925) and taught at the University of Cologne.
Willy Zinkgräf was an Indologist who studied under Max Walleser starting in 1922 and earned his Ph.D. at Heidelberg University by 1939. He held a post at the Walleser-Institut.

Sinologist Wilt L. Idema earned his degrees at Leiden University, completing his doctorate under Anthony François Paulus Hulsewé (~1968–1974). He served as Professor of Chinese Literature at Leiden (1976–1999) and Harvard University (2000–2013).

Winfred P. Lehmann worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (~1938–1941) and served as Professor emeritus at the University of Texas at Austin (~1986–2007).
Winfred Robert Martin was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. He served as Professor of Oriental Languages at Trinity College, Hartford, and as Librarian at the Hispanic Society of America.

Winfried Petri was a scholar of Indology, Tibetology, and history and archaeology. He earned his Ph.D. under Helmut Hoffmann at the University of Munich by 1966, later serving there as apl. Professor (1971) and director (1977–1979).

Wing-tsit Chan, a scholar of sinology and philosophy, studied at Harvard University (~1924–1929). He held academic posts at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (~1937–1942), Dartmouth College (~1942–1966), and Chatham University (~1966–1982).

Religious studies scholar Winnifred Fallers Sullivan studied at Cornell and the University of Chicago (J.D., Ph.D.). She held posts at Washington and Lee, Chicago (2000–2005), University at Buffalo (2006–2012), and Indiana University Bloomington (~2012).

Winston Kyan is a scholar of sinology, history and archaeology, and Buddhist studies. He completed his Ph.D. at the University of Chicago, where he studied under doctoral supervisor Hung Wu and Linda Seidel.

Winston L. King, a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies, studied at Asbury, Andover Newton, and Harvard (Ph.D. 1940). He held faculty posts at Grinnell College (1949–1964), Vanderbilt University (1964–1973), and Colorado State University (1973–1975).

Wladimir Zwalf was a scholar of Buddhist studies, history and archaeology, and Indology. He studied at Lincoln College under Thomas Burrow (1952–1955) and served as Assistant Keeper at the India Office Records and the British Museum (1962–1993).

Wm. Theodore de Bary was a scholar of sinology, philosophy, and Japanology. Educated at Columbia and Harvard, he served as Carpentier Professor of Oriental Studies at Columbia University (1953–2017) and president of the Association for Asian Studies (1969–1970).
Wojciech Marceli Gielecki, an Indologist and linguist, earned his Ph.D. at Jagiellonian University (~1896–1901) and served as a librarian there from ~1901 to 1939.

Wolfgang Adolf Theilkuhl was an Indologist who studied at the University of Hamburg (1919–1920) and earned his Ph.D. at the University of Munich (1918–1926). He served as a Lecturer at King's College London from 1828 to 1833.

Sinologist Wolfgang Franke studied at the University of Berlin and the University of Hamburg. He held academic posts at Sichuan University (~1945–1946) and Peking University (~1946–1948) before occupying the sinology chair at Hamburg (~1950–1977).

Wolfgang Krause was a linguist and Iranian and Central Asian scholar. Educated at Berlin and Göttingen under Wilhelm Schulze and Eduard Hermann, he held professorships in Indo-European linguistics at Königsberg (1929–1937) and Göttingen (1937–1963).

Wolfgang Lentz was a scholar of Iranian and Central Asian studies and linguistics. Educated at Munich and Göttingen, he worked at the Prussian Academy of Sciences (1924–1942) and became ordinary professor at the University of Hamburg (1964–1968).

Indologist Wolfgang Morgenroth completed his Ph.D. at Jena under Richard Hauschild and habilitated at Greifswald. He held professorships in comparative linguistics at Greifswald (1969–1972) and in Indology at Humboldt University of Berlin (1972–1994).
